difficultyReason: False dilemma / unstated premise flaw. The mayor presents two options — build the expressway or do nothing — without justifying the exhaustiveness of that dichotomy.
stimulus: Mayor: There has been a long debate in city council about how to accommodate projected increases in automobile traffic. Today, our choice is clear: either we adopt my plan to build a new expressway, or we do nothing. Doing nothing is not a viable option because our existing system of roads would be in gridlock within ten years given even a conservative estimate of future traffic levels. City council should therefore adopt my plan.
questionStem: The reasoning in the mayor's argument is most vulnerable to which one of the following criticisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It bases a projection only on conservative estimates rather than considering a wider range of estimates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It takes for granted that the options it considers are mutually exclusive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It fails to consider the possibility that the rate of increase in traffic will start to diminish after ten years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It fails to address the issue of the cost of traffic gridlock to the city's economy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It presents a choice that is limited to two options, without giving reasons for not considering any other options.

explanations.correct: The mayor says 'either we adopt my plan... or we do nothing' without justifying that those are the only options. Public transit, congestion pricing, road widening — any alternative breaks the dichotomy. That is a false-choice flaw.
explanations.A: Conservative estimates, if anything, strengthen the projection (even under favorable assumptions, gridlock happens).
explanations.B: The options are already exclusive — build-or-not-build. The issue is exhaustiveness, not exclusivity.
explanations.C: Even if the rate diminishes, the existing system would still gridlock.
explanations.D: Cost isn't the conclusion; adopting the plan is.

source.notes: Verbatim stimulus, stem, and choices from LSAC's 2015 Large Print LSAT sample PDF (section I, question 1). PDF is an unscored sample; LSAC does not publish the answer key for this booklet. Correct answer (E) inferred by analysis; an LSAC-published key would need to confirm.
